Description: explicit — omitted glyphs field, text renders in wrong font
prompt: My MapLibre GL JS stylesheet has no `glyphs` property set at all, and my symbol layers have `text-font` set to a font name. Text labels are showing up, but in a generic font, not the one I specified. Is this a bug I need to fix, or expected behavior? What's actually happening?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Short answer  
It’s **expected** behavior in MapLibre GL JS ≥ 5.11.0 when the style has **no `glyphs` field** the library falls back to the **local-font mode**: every name that appears in a layer’s `text-font` array is resolved the same way a browser resolves a CSS `font-family` list.  
If the browser can’t find a matching web-font (or a `font-faces` entry that points at a font file), it uses the platform’s default “sans-serif” font, which is why you see a generic typeface.

So it isn’t a bug – you just need to make sure the font you want is **available to the browser** and that the name you use in `text-font` matches the name you expose via one of the two supported mechanisms:

| Mechanism | What you do | When it works |
|-----------|-------------|---------------|
| **Web-font (`@font-face`)** | Declare the font in CSS (or load it with `document.fonts.load()`) and give it the exact name you use in `text-font`. | Works in any GL JS map, no `font-faces` entry needed. |
| **Style-level `font-faces`** | Add a `font-faces` object to the style JSON that maps the `text-font` name to a URL of a TTF/OTF (or WOFF/WOFF2) file, optionally limited by `unicode-range`. | Required when you want the same style to work on **MapLibre Native** (Android/iOS) or when you want to control which file is used without touching CSS. |

Below is a step-by-step guide to get the exact font you want rendered, plus a few common pitfalls and notes for Native.

---

## 1. What the engine is doing right now

1. **`glyphs` omitted** → GL JS switches to *local-font mode* (PR #4564).  
2. For each **code point** it needs, it asks the browser’s text layout engine to draw the glyph using the first matching font in the `text-font` list.  
3. If the browser **cannot find** a font with that exact name, it falls back to the OS default (usually “Arial”, “Helvetica”, or whatever the platform’s generic `sans-serif` resolves to).  
4. The map never tries to fetch a glyph PBF, so you see no network errors.

> **Native note** – MapLibre Native does **not** have this fallback. If you run the same style on Native, the absence of a `glyphs` URL will cause the text to disappear (or the whole tile to be considered missing). Keep a `glyphs` URL if you need cross-platform parity.

---

## 2. Getting the exact font you want on GL JS

### Option A – Load the font as a normal web-font

```css
/* style.css */
@font-face {
  font-family: "My Fancy Font";          /* must match text-font entry */
  src: url("https://example.com/fonts/MyFancyFont.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: normal;
  font-style: normal;
}
```

```js
// map initialization (after the CSS is loaded)
const map = new maplibregl.Map({
  container: "map",
  style: "https://example.com/style.json", // no glyphs field
  // other options …
});
```

**Why it works**

* The browser knows about `"My Fancy Font"` because of the `@font-face` rule.  
* When the style’s layer says  

  ```json
  "text-font": ["My Fancy Font", "Noto Sans Regular"]
  ```  

  the first entry resolves to the web-font you just declared, and the second is a fallback.

**Things to check**

| Check | How to verify |
|-------|----------------|
| Font file reachable (CORS, correct MIME) | Open the URL directly in the browser; look for `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header if it’s on a different origin. |
| Font name matches exactly (case-sensitive) | In Chrome DevTools → **Network → Font** you’ll see the request; the `font-family` in the CSS rule must be identical to the string in `text-font`. |
| Font loads before the map draws | If you create the map before the font is ready, the first render may use the fallback. Call `document.fonts.ready.then(() => map.setStyle(...))` or use `map.on('styledata', …)` after the font load promise resolves. |

### Option B – Declare the font in the style’s `font-faces` property

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "glyphs": "https://example.com/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",   // optional, can stay if you also need other fonts
  "font-faces": {
    "My Fancy Font": [
      {
        "url": "https://example.com/fonts/MyFancyFont-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0000-FFFF"]   // optional; omit to cover all code points
      }
    ]
  },
  "layers": [
    {
      "id": "place-labels",
      "type": "symbol",
      "layout": {
        "text-field": ["get", "name"],
        "text-font": ["My Fancy Font", "Noto Sans Regular"]
      },
      // …
    }
  ]
}
```

**Why it works**

* Both **MapLibre GL JS** (since 6.7.0) and **MapLibre Native** read `font-faces`.  
* The SDK downloads the TTF/OTF file itself (GL JS does it via XHR/fetch, Native via its own asset loader).  
* The font is then registered with the text shaping engine, and the name `"My Fancy Font"` becomes available for `text-font`.

**Things to check**

| Check | How to verify |
|-------|----------------|
| URL reachable & CORS-compatible (for GL JS) | Same as above – the browser must be able to fetch the file. |
| `unicode-range` covers the characters you need | If you limit the range too tightly, characters outside it will fall back to the next font in the list. |
| Font name matches exactly | The key in `font-faces` (`"My Fancy Font"` in the example) must be identical to the string in `text-font`. |
| Native asset path | On Android/iOS you can also point to a local file (`file:///android_asset/...`) – just make sure the URL scheme is one the native loader understands. |

---

## 3. Why you’re seeing a *generic* font right now

1. **No `glyphs` URL** → GL JS uses the local-font path.  
2. **No web-font or `font-faces` entry** that matches `"My Fancy Font"` → the browser falls back to its default `sans-serif`.  
3. The map therefore renders correctly (text is there) but with the wrong visual style.

That’s exactly what the skill describes under **“GL JS local-font fallback”**.

---

## 4. Optional: Keep a `glyphs` URL for cross-platform consistency

If you want the same style to look identical on both GL JS **and** Native **without** relying on the local-font fallback, add a `glyphs` URL that serves the same font as a PBF set:

```json
{
  "glyphs": "https://myselfhosted.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
  "font-faces": { … }   // optional, still useful for complex scripts
}
```

*You can copy the pre-built Noto glyph PBF tree from the OpenMapTiles `fonts` repo or from `https://demotiles.maplibre.org/font/` and host it yourself.*  
When the style has a `glyphs` field, GL JS will **prefer** those PBFs for all scripts **except** CJK ideographs (which are still rendered locally unless you set `localIdeographFontFamily: false`).  

---

## 5. Quick checklist to fix your map

| ✅ | Action |
|---|--------|
| **1** | Verify that the font you want is either (a) declared with `@font-face` in CSS **or** (b) listed in the style’s `font-faces` object. |
| **2** | Make sure the **name** you use in `text-font` matches the font-family name exactly (case-sensitive, spaces included). |
| **3** | Ensure the font file URL is reachable from the browser (CORS headers, correct MIME type). |
| **4** | If you need the same look on Native, add a `glyphs` URL that serves the font as PBFs (or keep the `font-faces` entry – Native reads it from 11.13.0 / 6.18.0 onward). |
| **5** | (Optional) If you want CJK characters to use the same custom font, set `localIdeographFontFamily: false` **and** provide a glyph PBF set for the CJK font. This is slower and usually unnecessary. |
| **6** | Reload the page, open DevTools → **Network → Font** to confirm the correct font file is being fetched, and verify the map now shows the intended typeface. |

---

## 6. TL;DR for your specific case

*Your map is working as designed.*  
Because `glyphs` is omitted, GL JS falls back to the browser’s font system. Since the font you referenced in `text-font` isn’t available as a web-font or via `font-faces`, the browser uses its generic fallback, giving you the “generic font” you see.

**Fix it** by either:

1. **Loading the font with CSS** (`@font-face`) **or**  
2. **Adding a `font-faces` entry** that points at the TTF/OTF file, **or**  
3. **Providing a glyph-PBF server** (and a `glyphs` URL) if you also need Native parity.

No bug to report – just a missing font resource.  

--- 

### Further reading

* **MapLibre GL JS local-font fallback** – PR #4564, changelog 5.11.0.  
* **`font-faces` spec** – <https://maplibre.org/maplibre-style-spec/root/#font-faces>  
* **Web-font example** – <https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/examples/style-labels-with-web-fonts/>  
* **Local-fonts example** – <https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/examples/style-labels-with-local-fonts/>  

If you follow the checklist and still see the wrong typeface, open the browser console, look for warnings like *“Unable to load glyph range … Rendering codepoint U+… locally instead.”* – that indicates the fallback path is still being used because the font name wasn’t resolved. Adjust the name or the font-face definition and you’ll be good to go.

Description: anti-pattern — porting a Native font-faces config to GL JS
prompt: I have a working `font-faces` config in my MapLibre Native app's stylesheet that renders local fonts offline with explicit Unicode ranges per file. I'm now building a MapLibre GL JS web app and want the same offline-font behavior — can I copy the same `font-faces` config into my GL JS stylesheet?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
## Short answer  
**Yes – you can reuse the same `font-faces` block in a MapLibre GL JS style**, but you have to meet a few GL JS-specific requirements:

| Requirement | What to do |
|-------------|------------|
| **GL JS version** | Use **≥ 6.7.0** (the version that first reads `font-faces`). |
| **Reachable URLs** | The `url` values must be HTTP(S) URLs that the browser can fetch (relative to the page, CDN, or a Service-Worker-cached asset). File-system paths that work on Native won’t work in the browser. |
| **CORS** | If the fonts are on a different origin, serve them with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or the page’s origin). |
| **Offline support** | Cache the font files (e.g. via a Service Worker, `Cache-Storage`, or by bundling them as data-URIs) so the browser can still load them when the network is unavailable. |
| **Glyphs URL** | Either **omit** the `glyphs` field (GL JS will fall back to local-font rendering) **or** keep it – the `font-faces` entries will be used for the scripts they cover, and the glyph server will be consulted for everything else. |
| **Runtime changes** | If you need to swap the `font-faces` after the map is created, call `map.setFontFaces(newObject)`; otherwise the static block in the style is enough. |

Below is a step-by-step guide, plus a few gotchas you’ll hit when moving from Native to the browser.

---

## 1️⃣ Make sure you’re on a recent GL JS build  

```html
<script src="https://unpkg.com/maplibre-gl@6.15.0/dist/maplibre-gl.js"></script>
<link href="https://unpkg.com/maplibre-gl@6.15.0/dist/maplibre-gl.css" rel="stylesheet" />
```

*Versions < 6.7.0 silently ignore `font-faces`.*  
If you’re using a bundled version (e.g. via Webpack), check `package.json` or `npm list maplibre-gl`.

---

## 2️⃣ Copy the `font-faces` block verbatim  

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "glyphs": "https://example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",   // optional
  "font-faces": {
    "Noto Sans Regular": [
      {
        "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF", "U+0100-024F"]
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans Devanagari": [
      {
        "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"]
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans Arabic": [
      {
        "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF"]
      }
    ]
  },
  "layers": [ … ]
}
```

*What changed?*  
Only the **URL scheme** may need tweaking:

| Native style | GL JS style |
|--------------|-------------|
| `file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf` | `https://mydomain.com/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf` (or `./fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf` if you serve it from the same origin) |
| `file:///ios_bundle/fonts/...` | same as above |

If you want a **truly offline** page (no network at all), you can embed the fonts as **data URIs**:

```json
{
  "url": "data:font/ttf;base64,AAEAAAARAQAABAA…"
}
```

(Only practical for a handful of small fonts; otherwise use a Service Worker.)

---

## 3️⃣ Cache the fonts for offline use  

### Option A – Service Worker (recommended)

```js
self.addEventListener('install', e => {
  e.waitUntil(
    caches.open('maplibre-fonts').then(cache => {
      return cache.addAll([
        '/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf',
        '/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf',
        '/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf'
      ]);
    })
  );
});

self.addEventListener('fetch', e => {
  if (e.request.url.endsWith('.ttf')) {
    e.respondWith(caches.match(e.request).then(resp => resp || fetch(e.request)));
  }
});
```

Now the browser will serve the font from the cache even when the network is down.

### Option B – Pre-bundle with Webpack / Vite

```js
import NotoSansRegular from './fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf?url';
```

Webpack will emit the file and replace the import with a URL that points to the bundled asset (still an HTTP URL, but served from the same origin).

---

## 4️⃣ Decide what to do with the `glyphs` field  

| Scenario | Recommended setting |
|----------|----------------------|
| **Pure offline** (no glyph server) | **Omit** `glyphs` entirely. GL JS will render every `text-font` entry locally via TinySDF (or via the browser’s text engine for complex scripts). |
| **Hybrid** (you have a glyph server for Latin, but want custom Devanagari, Arabic, etc.) | Keep `glyphs` pointing at your server. The `font-faces` entries will *override* the glyphs for the Unicode ranges you declared. Anything outside those ranges falls back to the glyph server. |
| **CJK** | Leave `glyphs` as you like; GL JS will **ignore** `text-font` for ideographs and use `localIdeographFontFamily` (default `sans-serif`). If you want a specific on-device CJK font, set `localIdeographFontFamily` in the map options. |

```js
const map = new maplibregl.Map({
  container: 'map',
  style: 'style.json',
  localIdeographFontFamily: '"Noto Sans CJK SC", sans-serif' // optional, improves CJK look
});
```

---

## 5️⃣ Verify it works  

1. Open the page **with DevTools → Network** throttled to “Offline”.  
2. Look for the font requests (`*.ttf`, `*.otf`). They should be served from the Service Worker cache (status 200 (OK) from cache).  
3. Check the map’s labels:  
   * Latin text → rendered from the local font (or from the glyph server if you kept it).  
   * Devanagari, Arabic, etc. → rendered from the `font-faces` files.  
   * CJK → rendered by the browser’s built-in ideograph engine (or the family you set).  

If any label falls back to a generic system font, open the console – you’ll see warnings like:

```
Unable to load glyph range ... Rendering codepoint U+0905 locally instead.
```

That means the glyph PBF for that range failed to load (or you omitted `glyphs`). In that case the browser’s fallback font is used, which is exactly what you want for offline mode.

---

## 6️⃣ Gotchas & troubleshooting rows  

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| **No text appears at all** | `glyphs` omitted **and** the browser cannot fetch any `font-faces` URL (404 or CORS). | Verify the URLs are reachable, add proper CORS headers, or embed as data URIs. |
| **Latin text looks different from Native** | GL JS is using the **local-font fallback** (TinySDF) because the glyph PBF failed or `glyphs` is omitted. | Keep a working `glyphs` URL for Latin, or serve the exact same PBF set you used on Native. |
| **Devanagari letters are split into separate glyphs** | Using a GL JS version **< 6.7.0** (no grapheme-cluster rendering). | Upgrade to ≥ 6.7.0. |
| **Arabic appears left-to-right** | Using GL JS < 6.9.0 **and** didn’t load the RTL plugin. | Upgrade to ≥ 6.9.0 (plugin deprecated) or load `setRTLTextPlugin` before map creation. |
| **CJK characters look blocky** | `localIdeographFontFamily` is set to a low-resolution system font. | Set it to a higher-quality on-device font (e.g. `"Noto Sans CJK SC", sans-serif`). |
| **Fonts load slowly on first page view** | Not cached yet. | Pre-cache fonts in the Service Worker `install` event, or embed them as data URIs. |

---

## 7️⃣ TL;DR checklist for copying `font-faces` from Native → GL JS  

1. **Upgrade** to MapLibre GL JS ≥ 6.7.0.  
2. **Copy** the `font-faces` block verbatim, **changing any `file://` URLs to HTTP(S) URLs** that the browser can reach.
